code.originalText: Fifteen-week review after the eight-week omeprazole course: on-demand therapy, sleep, the remedy, and mood

text.paragraph: Fifteen-week review: on-demand omeprazole, sleep, the remedy, and mood. [S]

Mr. Aurelius returns six weeks after finishing the eight-week omeprazole course. He has taken omeprazole on demand about once a week, after a late dinner, and has had no chest or epigastric pain otherwise. His appetite is good and he has regained most of the weight he had lost. He has finished six CBT-I sessions and sleeps about six and a half hours, falling asleep within twenty minutes. About four weeks ago he chose to take the herbal paste on only two nights a week, a smaller amount, and noticed only a night or two of lighter sleep. He has no craving and takes no more on the nights he uses it. The COVID-19 illness in July left no after-effects. He says he feels clearer in the mornings and is working shorter evenings. [S]

tr.td: Well; weight 65.0 kg, BMI 22.0; pulse 70, blood pressure 118/76

Burning and pressing pain in the upper abdomen and lower chest after meals, for more than a year and worse over three months, with poor appetite, waking at night with pain and a sour taste, and a 3 kg weight loss; not brought on by exertion; normal ECG; cardiac and peptic causes to be excluded
S — Synthetic presenting concern at the index visit, superseded by the diagnosis at endoscopy; its pattern echoes the stomach and chest complaints and the pain with food that Dio describes (D).

Gastroesophageal reflux disease with erosive esophagitis, Los Angeles grade B, and a 2 cm sliding hiatal hernia; Helicobacter pylori negative on biopsy; coronary disease excluded by CT coronary angiography; synthetic modern diagnosis for his documented stomach and chest complaints
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis; the cause of his real complaints is unknown and no historical diagnosis is made.

Daily use of an unregulated opium-containing herbal remedy for about six years, for stomach pain and sleep; opioid use disorder criteria not met (one DSM-5-TR criterion, restlessness and poor sleep when he stopped it); expected physiological dependence; constipation and possibly slowed gastric emptying from the opioid
S — Synthetic modern finding anchored to the theriac he took (D); no opioid use disorder or addiction is attributed to him (the claim is disputed, R).
Chronic insomnia disorder for more than a year, with waking from night pain and trouble returning to sleep; Insomnia Severity Index 17 (moderate)

list.item:
Reflux esophagitis, healed clinically, on on-demand therapy (K21.00). Grade B esophagitis treated for eight weeks with resolution of symptoms; on-demand omeprazole about once a week controls the occasional heartburn after late meals. No alarm features, so no repeat endoscopy; manometry and reflux monitoring are not needed while he is well. [S]
Omeprazole on demand; return if heartburn comes back most days, for a trial of daily therapy at the lowest dose.
Keep the early evening meal.

Chronic insomnia, in remission after CBT-I (G47.00). Insomnia Severity Index 7, below the threshold for clinical insomnia, after six sessions. [S]
Keep the fixed rising time and the sleep-diary skills; a booster session if sleep slips.

Opium-containing remedy, about two nights a week by his choice (F11.90). He has reduced his use step by step at his own pace and is sleeping better with less of it. No DSM-5-TR criterion is present now. The paste is still unregulated and of unknown strength. [S]
Any further change is his decision; the clinic will support stopping, staying where he is, or a slow taper.
Never a larger amount after nights off; naloxone at the bedside.
A urine drug test again in a year, with his consent; review at each visit.

Strain of command and mood (Z56.6). PHQ-9 3 and GAD-7 3, down from 8 and 6 at intake. [S]
Keep the protected evening hours.

Constipation from the opioid (K59.03). Rarely needs the laxative now that he takes the remedy less often. [S]
Polyethylene glycol as needed.
